init_text: It's about treating another person regardless of their gender as you would like to be treated yourself. It's really that simple. Think of the other as equal. Respect sometimes can be a very weird word. Because respect is something I genuinely feel that you have to earn. It's not a compulsory blind, you know what I mean, or a prerequisite. I mean, if somebody is, in your opinion, is not somebody who treats other people well, you don't have to respect that person. I mean, you can have lesser respect for that person because that person is not a good person. But treating somebody as an equal, somebody that you don't, and especially people that you don't know. Everything is so divided, whether it's status. We have so many in where we are, where we live. Whether it's status, whether it's religion, whether it's caste, everything comes with its share of how someone should be treated depending on who they are and where they are in their life. You know, so you're from a very young age constantly either in somewhere in the middle of this spectrum of feeling powerful or not, because maybe depending on where you are, where you're born, who you are, somebody is considered more powerful than you already, just by birth, you know, or then you're at the top of the food chain, because just by birth, you've done nothing, right? But you're just considered and that's how you're treated. And that kind of stuff has to stop. Because that's what gives you that feeling of entitlement, of feeling like, I mean, everything is for me. I'm the catch whiskers. Or then you're in a place where you feel you have no power. So to exert some fake sense of power, you will trample upon people who you consider less powerful than you. That's what's going to happen. So I mean, it's a matter of education. It's a matter of just changing social construct, I feel. Something has to change because we are born, we are weirdly enough born into power dynamics. We are born into a system that exists, which puts you in a place and either makes you a minority or makes you a this or makes you a that. You know what I mean? And then the world treats you accordingly. It has nothing to do with your character. It has nothing to do with merit. It has nothing to do with anything else. init_text: So, you know, there's this reality which I found really interesting. There's a trend on social media where men are making an argument saying, if you are not willing as a woman to pay me dowry, I will not pay you alimony. And this is a very popular statement. What's your response to that?
resp_text: I'll answer this by giving a very basic legal argument and then I'll deal with the social argument. Dowry is a reflection of a woman being treated as a commodity. Dowry is demanded and it's illegal. We have laws against dowry in India. Why is it illegal? What's the social rationale? The reason is that a woman is accepted not for what she is as a member of the family, but because she brings in a certain amount of wealth and that she's treated as a burden. And therefore, you know, this payment or this, you know, commodification of a woman is implicit in the whole dowry culture, which is wrong. Now, alimony does not make a commodity of a woman. If a man and a woman who are together separate, and the court orders the payment of alimony to her, that is for the reason that if they have been, say, married for 20 years, and the couple then separates, or even five years, but the woman in the meantime has had children, She's been out of work. She can't just get back to work and, you know, suddenly start becoming a member of the workforce if she has not been working all these years because she's devoted the most productive years of her life to bringing up a family, to looking after parents, parents-in-law, the children, child-rearing, everything that happens in every strata of our society. So alimony in that sense is to enable a woman to live a life of dignity, even after she loses the comfort of a home, the matrimonial home, and to ensure that she's not exposed to the elements. Now, the amount of alimony would obviously differ from case to case. For instance, suppose the woman who is asking for alimony is a high-tech, highly educated member of the force, of the workforce. The court would say, hey, but even after you're divorced, aren't you capable of standing out there in the workplace and holding your own? You're entitled to earn your own income. You have a good job. You know, you have your own means of survival. So why should we order alimony? So it's not, the law is not that the moment a man and woman divorce, that the woman gets alimony at the expense of the man. That's a very wrong assessment.

resp_text: Now, why is this insulation for judges created by our constitution? It was created when the constitution was adopted with a great deal of care. The reason why judges are insulated is for the reason that they should not depend either on any political opinion or for that matter on any segment of society for their legitimacy or for their existence as judges. And judges are intended to apply, when they decide constitutional cases, the fundamental principles of the Constitution, which are to have everlasting presence in society. It's certain eternal values of the Constitution. If judges were elected, for instance, as they are in some parts of the world, in the United States, several judges across the states are elected, which means that periodically they have to go back to their electorate and ask for votes. And that's obviously going to impact upon the kind of decisions which they take. Our constitution didn't adopt that model for a valid reason, that they didn't want judges who would be dependent for their existence as judges on a popular or political mandate. The principle, therefore, is that judges are accountable to the law. Judges are accountable to the constitution. Now, if a judge is guilty of a misdemeanor, all right, which is a separate issue altogether, they are subject to a mechanism for accountability, which the Constitution and the law have provided. But this insulation of judges was brought in for a very valid reason and a justification to sort of liberate them from any particular segment of popular opinion or belief. and to allow them that freedom to decide cases, uninfluenced by, you know, any dominant or other political opinion or sentiment. For instance, when a law is passed, Judges are aware of the fact as a matter of principle, not just as practice, that the law has been enacted by our legislators, whether in the states or in the members of Parliament in Parliament. And that law is enacted by people who owe allegiance to the people. They're elected democratically and they are empowered by the Constitution to enact laws. So we wouldn't strike down a law merely because I have a different view of the law or the wisdom of the law.

resp_text: There are cases, there are two different types of cases. The first is a situation where there is no law on the subject, where the court has a greater deal of latitude or, you know, an authority to sort of fashion guidelines, particularly the Supreme Court, because the Supreme Court has the power under Article 142 to do something which would be in aid of substantive justice. Now, one area, for instance, where there was no law on the subject was the prevention of sexual harassment in the workplace. So, when the judgment in Vishakha's case was delivered by the Supreme Court, they relied, therefore, on international law. The Convention on the Elimination of Discrimination Against Women, CEDAW, or basic constitutional principles. That's one area where there's no law on the subject. Second area is where there is a law on the subject. Where there is a law on the subject, that law can be challenged if that law is unconstitutional. If that law can be challenged on the ground that it breaches our fundamental rights, say the right to equality or the right to freedom of speech and expression. What can the court do? The court can strike down the law, it can uphold the law. If it strikes down the law, the court cannot enact a new law. The reenactment of the law is then left to parliament or the state legislatures as the case may be. Now, in the marriage equality case, there was a law and there is a law, namely the Special Marriage Act. Now, the Special Marriage Act was a visionary piece of legislation which was enacted in the 1950s to allow for couples who belong to different faiths to get married. So it gave a secular platform for couples, a man and a woman who belong to different faiths to get married. Now the law expressly uses, specifically uses the expression man and woman. There's a different age of consent for a man, 21, a different age of consent for a woman, 18. You know, we have degrees of prohibited relationships in the law. For instance, you can't marry your sister or brother, right? Yes. So there are different degrees of prohibited relationships which are created for a man by that law and for a woman by that law. Next, you have different principles for succession in a marital situation. The problem which the Supreme Court faced in the marriage equality case was that no one wanted the Special Marriage Act to be struck down, because if you strike it down, you'll deprive couples belonging to different faiths of the only basis on which you can get married under the law. So striking down the law was out of question. Nobody was even asking for that. What the petitioners really sought was this, that essentially, though the law uses the expression man and woman, read the word man and woman, instead of that, read man and man, woman and woman. We said that is not something which the court can do.

It's something which I've thought of. The importance of courts is not just in terms of the decisions which you take, but it's a space for a dialogue. In a political democracy, this is not just a place where people come with their problems and get decisions. Now with, you know, virtual hearings, live streaming of court proceedings, the outreach of the court is not just to those 200 people in the courtroom or those who read the newspapers, but now it's across millions of people who are seeing what is being heard in the court. prev_text: You know, talking of the collision, when people criticize the collision, my answer is basically this. What system would be better than what we have at present? Would we want a situation, would we like to have a design parameter in terms of which appointments to the higher judiciary like the High Courts and the Supreme Court would be made by the government? Obviously no, because you want independent judges. So when we criticize any existing system, and I'm dealing with the criticism of the collision, I'm not here to defend any system. We have to understand what's a better alternative. If one alternative, people say, is to have outside talent into the decision-making process, that is people from civil society who will come into the decision-making process apart from the judges, who will appoint them to those bodies? The devil lies in the fine print. So if you give the power to appoint, say, independent people from outside, again to the government, will those people who are appointing... They will be government appointees. Right. Now, therefore, if you are talking of an alternate system or a better system, How should that system be designed? What do we want to achieve? We ultimately want to achieve a process which is efficient, where judicial vacancies are not left unfilled over a long period of time. Second, you want judges who are independent, judges who are qualified and judges who are appointed on merit having due regard to the need for diversity. diversity in terms of gender, diversity in terms of region, diversity in terms of bringing different groups into society, particularly marginalized groups. Now, I'll now deal with the issue of transparency, which you raised. Absolutely, I completely agree with you, and I tried to do that as a judge of the Supreme Court and later on as a Chief Justice of India. Transparency at an objective level requires that you put out into the public realm the principles on the basis of which you make your decisions. Now, when I was Chief Justice of India, we put out onto the website of the Supreme Court, the principles which we adopt in recommending people for appointment to the Supreme Court. The first principle which you follow is seniority, because the available pool of talent consists of judges from the high courts, the Chief Justices and other judges of the high court. And you, of course, have a few bar judges who come in from the Supreme Court bar or the high court bar for that matter. So the first principle is of seniority. Your pool, you look at, say, the first 50. It's not like an inflexible yardstick, but you look at the senior most. They may be the chief justices of the high court. They may be the senior judges of the high court. You don't go to a judge whose serial number is 50 in the order of seniority, because there are people who have led their lives in service of the institution. You can't completely displace their legitimate expectations of at least being considered for high judicial office. So seniority is the first criteria. not the most important, but one of the criteria. The second is merit. Now, how do you assess the merit of judges? In the collision, when I was Chief Justice of India, we would circulate to all the members of the collision judgments of those judges who are under consideration in a pen drive. And those judgments would be assessed by the members of the collegium. We see judgments of the high court judges constantly. As I said on Mondays and Fridays, you're constantly looking at judgments. But then as a collegium, everybody looks at the same judgments together. In the high courts, the process of assessment is a little different. The collegium in the high court consists of the Chief Justice and the two CNMO judges. There is a Judgment Assessment Committee. So, when district judges are appointed as judges of the High Court, there is a Judgment Assessment Committee which actually grades the judgments of the High Court judges. In the Supreme Court, when we assess High Court judges who are to be appointed to the Supreme Court, the judgments of those judges are circulated to the judges of the Collegium. So, the second principle is merit. Have they done some exceptional work? Are they good in disposals? The third consideration is the need for diversity. And this was all put out onto the website of the Supreme Court. Diversity in what terms? Diversity of having more women into the Indian Judiciary, into the Supreme Court. Diversity in ensuring that this does not become just a privilege of, you know, the elite, because that's one of the criticisms. So diversity of people coming in from marginalized backgrounds, the scheduled castes, the scheduled tribes, people come belonging to the backward classes, people belonging to minorities. So you must have representatives. There's no quota in the Supreme Court or in the High Court. Yes. But you must have this broad representation. Why? Representation, next important criterion, representation to different regions and high courts in India. You have different states, you have different High Courts. Now the larger High Courts, say like the High Court of Judicature at Allahabad, the Bombay High Court, the Calcutta High Court may have more than one representative just because of the dimensions of that state. A huge state. 160 judges is the strength of the Allahabad High Court. 90 plus judges is the strength of the Bombay High Court. So you typically will have more than one. Delhi High Court will have more than one judge representing that high court. Now again, that's not a quota. Northeast. You know, now, merely because you want representation of different high courts, you're not bringing to the Supreme Court a judge who is just one year into the bench.
init_text: Right.
resp_text: Because there are some high courts which are very young high courts. You know, judges are very young because they have, say, five judges in that high court. Your progression is much slower. So that's another very important criterion, giving broad representation in the Supreme Court to diverse regions in the country, diverse high courts. Now, to what level do you provide for transparency in discussing the names? Next step, will you also discuss everything pertaining to that person? Because in the High Courts you do a 360 degree assessment. You are looking at their personal lives, you are looking at their personal incomes, you are looking at the volume of cases which they have done. See, someone at the bar who has a divorce case pending, there may be certain serious allegations about that person. You may or may not treat those allegations as true. But if you're putting out everything about the personal lives of individuals in the public realm, then there is a grave danger that good people will not accept judgeship because they will just not want to barter their privacy or their own personal dignity into this scrutiny in the name of transparency. So while transparency is a desirable constitutional goal and a public interest goal because people have a vital interest in knowing how these appointments are being made. And I take the point that as citizens today, I'm a citizen, you're a citizen, we want to know why was this particular person appointed to the bench. But then if we start, you know, crossing boundaries and start looking at the personal lives of individuals, the dangerous good people will just say, sorry, I don't want to put everything of my own personal life, I'll put it before the collision. But I don't want to put it, you know, for public debate and for people to have an unnecessary curiosity into every facet of my personal existence. resp_text: The difference is that In India, let's speak just about India right now. In India, couture is mainly bridal wear. The couture definition is something couture could be customary, even a suit could be couture, you know. Or you see couture as something very handmade, something very crafted, but in India everything is handmade, right? Or machine made, but it's all, you know. How you make it, the finishing, the embroidery, the solidness of it doesn't really matter. It might not even last out. But couture is something that has to be timeless. So the craftsmanship of it, the embroidery, the making of it is something that has to be timeless. So there are two different worlds in that sense. init_text: And how was the shooting experience?
resp_text: The shooting experience was very different. The way you get to listen to the script, the way the music is from the panchayat, such a good, melodious music comes. And the shooting experience is completely different. What was the experience? Because we are shooting there in May, June and April. Mostly, I don't know how, we get stuck in the same weather and there the temperature is between 45 to 47 degrees. And in the first season, we were shooting in 45-47 degrees cold. Because we had to show 26th January, in which everyone is in shawls and sweaters. And in season 1, we shot in a little bit of heat, so there were no ACs in the sets. So that was a very dangerous experience. And we know that it is very difficult to shoot in villages. Because all three or four things there are very extreme. If it is cold, it will be very cold. If it rains, if it is a night shoot, there will be so many mosquitoes there that you cannot shoot. There will be so many mosquitoes throughout in the frame. So to save yourself from that, put some medicine. And then the smell of that... And it's a different story when it comes to summers. And you are shooting in the cold. You are shooting in the cold, wearing a sweater. So that's very... I think for everyone, I mean for the whole crew. Because everyone, I mean the whole crew goes from Mumbai. 150 people go and settle in that village. And they settle in a separate city. So, but gradually I got used to it. I think everyone got to know how to live here. And who is going to get irritated at what time. So, I got used to it. But it took time. It was a very difficult shoot. But yes, I think to make something fun, you have to face some difficulty. You don't get anything so easily. So to shoot that fun, you had to bear a lot of things.

init_text: Which one day do you particularly remember that this is a memory from season 1?
resp_text: Season one, I think day one was a roller coaster. I think it was a long shoot. It was a 9 to 9 shift. So we were shooting a chunk of the night scene. And I was meeting all the senior actors for the first time. Raghu sir, Neena ma'am, everyone. I was a fan of them. So I was nervous to perform in front of them. It was so hot from 7 to 8 in the morning. And we were shooting in the cold on the first day. We were shooting in sweaters on the first day. So that was the reality that this is how it's going to be for a month and a half. And then the weather got cold at night. And the mood was also good. Because it was cold, so the mood was good. We were doing a scene in which Nina ma'am's character was frying puris and we were eating. So, Raghu sir has a habit. If he laughs once, he doesn't stop. Then he goes on a trip. Then he doesn't stop. Then he won't get the shot. Then it will take him time. It will take him 1-1.5 hours. If Raghu sir laughs on the set. So, it is very difficult to stop his laughter. So, that day he laughed at something. And she kept on laughing. She kept on laughing for half an hour. As soon as the dialogue came, she started laughing. Very cutely. And everyone started laughing. Then Nina ma'am scolded her. She said, do it, man. Go home. So she said, yes, yes, I'll do it. So that way, it was a very interesting day. We got to know everyone. And we got to know everything about the weather. That yes, this is going to be difficult. It's going to be tough.

init_text: And then, as the lockdown was lifted, life returned to normal. Was the work going according to that? Did it increase? Or you were saying no actively, that I don't want to do this.
resp_text: Yes, the things that I didn't like instinctively, according to me. According to me, I was thinking that I don't know how it will be executed, how will I do it. So I don't give a lot of suggestions that can we do this or that in this. Because I think it's the story of the writer and the director. They want to say it in their own way. So I just have to say that I want to be a part of it or not. I don't tell you to mold it like this or do it my way. It's not my job to tell you that. And I think it's wrong. Of course, it can work at some time. But it's a wrong way. Whether you are interested in what the writer wants to say or not. I think you should commit only if you are interested in what the director wants to say. Otherwise, there is no need to commit. I have learned a lot from those experiences. Commit fully once you are interested. If you are not interested, you are thinking that I will do something like this, later I will talk and do something, later there is a problem in this scene, later I will talk and solve it. Then it becomes very difficult. If you do the work, then do it. Otherwise, you can get stuck. So, it will come with experience. If you are interested, then do it. So, the things that I was not interested in, I was refusing. But yes, the work grew a lot after that. But the lockdowns were very unpredictable. Two and a half years, sometimes it was happening, then sometimes the work was starting. So, due to that, there were problems. It's not like some things, like Jadugar stopped in the middle for a long time. 4-5 months. I mean, we shot for 20 days, then stopped for 5 months. Then we shot for a month and a half later. And similarly, there is a sad moment. We have to deal with it. But it is not worth entering a zone of disappointment, disgracement and becoming very depressed or becoming dysfunctional. We have to deal with distress without becoming depressed and dysfunctional. Deal with it. So one will not become overwhelmed by it. Yes, we have to deal with happiness and distress, although we are spiritually elevated. Just because I read Bhagavad Gita, that does not mean mosquitoes will not bite me. That does not mean I will not sweat if I stand in the sun for a long time. But happiness and distress are there in a monk's life also, in a spiritually elevated sage's life also and an average person's life also. But when we have that spiritual wisdom with us, we will not get overwhelmed. We will not get unduly affected. We will have the ability our maturity to reconcile it internally, reconcile it philosophically. We have to externally address the situation as far as humanly possible and we have to internally reconcile the situation philosophically, rationally. That external addressing of the situation while internally reconciling the situation shows how mature we are. And Gita gives us that maturity.

resp_text: Purpose is twofold. One is the immediate purpose. Second is the ultimate purpose. Immediate purpose is for our self-preservation. Ultimate purpose is self-realization. So how do we do justice to our pursuits for both immediate success and ultimate success or self-preservation and self-realization when we have self-awareness? So self-preservation in this term that self is body. So, as long as I am living in this body, I need to work for the maintenance of this body. I need to earn my livelihood. I need to work hard to get some money and then maintain my life and maintain the family. So, that is self-preservation. And self-preservation is the immediate duty, immediate need, immediate purpose of everyone. No doubt about it. But am I supposed to just work hard for my livelihood, whole life? Is that the only purpose of my life? Should I just work hard, get money, and then eat food, sleep, and then next day morning again go, work hard, and get money, and maintain myself? Is that the only purpose of my life? So we need to question ourselves. Who am I? So, am I this body? This is my hand. This is hand and this is my hand, but I am not this hand. This is my head and I am not head. This is leg and it is my leg. I am not the leg. So, it is my body, my hand, my leg, my head, my eyes. Means who is that I? This is gross body. I just spoke about the gross body and I am not the gross body. This gross body belongs to me and behind this gross body is a subtle body. And that subtle body has mind, intelligence and ego. Oftentimes, people may not be able to differentiate between what is mind, what is intelligence, what is ego. They say ego is born out of mind or mind is born out of ego or intelligence and mind are same. They may have a lot of confusion. Basically, mind is that faculty within us that stores all desires, thoughts, emotions, feelings. But the mind does not have the ability to analyze. Intelligence is that faculty within us that analyzes whether the mind's thoughts are good or bad, beneficial or non-beneficial, or destructive or constructive, useful or useless. Intelligence does the discrimination part. Then comes the ego. Ego is oftentimes seen or perceived in a negative sense only. But ego basically means a sense of identity, who am I, a sense of identity. So I may be a teacher or a student or a doctor or an employee or employee of a company or a plumber or a carpenter or a builder. So these are all different identities and everyone should have some identity in the society for smooth function. that is not the only identity. Today's student can become tomorrow's teacher. Today's maestri who works for the construction of a building can tomorrow become an architect. Today's lawyer can become a judge tomorrow. Today's doctor can become a patient tomorrow. So, these roles keep changing. We need to have a sense of identity, but they are changing identities. Now, when we overly identify ourselves with those designations, temporary designations, what happens is that leads to a sense of pride and arrogance and that is the ego that people commonly refer to. Ego is basically a sense of identity, but that sense of identity can create some superiority complex or inferiority complex, pride or envy. And that is seen as ego, which is correct, of course, it is a fairly good understanding. But I would say more precisely that is called false ego. You have a sense of identity, when you overly identify yourself with a position or a designation or a role and become proud or envious, that is called false ego. That is a symptom of false ego. But apart from that, there is a true ego. There is a real ego. There is a real sense of identity. What is my real identity? My real identity is I am a child of God. This is called self-awareness. I talked about gross body, which is visible, which has visible limbs of hands and legs and eyes, etc. And behind this gross body is a subtle body that has mind, intelligence and ego. All three are material. They are not visible to the eyes, but they exist. Right? So behind this gross and subtle material bodies is the spirit soul. And that spirit soul is a child of God. Krishna says in Bhagavad Gita, All Jivas, all living beings are my amshas, they are my children. Right? So that is our original identity and that is called self-awareness. I spoke about three terms in the beginning of the answer. Preservation, Self-awareness and Self-realisation. So Self-preservation is the immediate purpose, that is bodily maintenance. And Self-realisation is the ultimate purpose. When I realise myself as a child of God, when I realise my eternal connection with God, what is my role as a God's servant, as a God's child? So, that question we need to ask that is self-realization, that is the ultimate purpose. And what connects this self-preservation and self-realization, what connects this immediate purpose and ultimate purpose is that self-awareness. And that self-awareness comes by sincerely reading wisdom text and associating with wise people. For me, it is reading Bhagavad Gita and associating with other devotees in my ISKCON community. So we need to work for our immediate purpose, no doubt about it. And we should also endeavor to fulfill our ultimate purpose of self-realization. Does it answer your question? Yes. On purpose.

init_text: Would it be fair to say that your task that you had given yourself in the late 1990s was completed through encounters?
resp_text: Not at all. Cinema and the other guys have made a myth. The so-called encounter specialists glorified themselves so that they could also do a bit of money-making business and they brought disrepute to themselves. Frankly speaking, it's a combination of so many factors. One is 1600 man years of criminals was put behind the bars by using MPDA. It's a detention act where the police commissioner can detain a criminal under certain conditions for one year. It is subject to the government super ruling and also the high court. Within 12 days he can appeal to the government and after 12 days he can go to high court in a petition, writ petition and they review whether it is right or wrong, they release, they can castigate, sometimes they can punish you also. That was there for long years but that wasn't used well effectively. So when I came, We detained 1600 criminals for one year. So that means 1600 man years behind the bars. Crime has to come down. Took them off the streets. Took them off, put them behind the bars. From there can they shoot? No. So that was one. Second is the weapons which was floating. Free floating of illegal weapons. 2600 weapons we recovered. In 2 years and 9 months. 3 years let's say approximately. We recovered. So anybody who came and met you took out a gun first and said aata bol no? So that I made a statement in the newspaper saying that anybody who takes an illegal weapon from his holster should not be alive to make use of it later. Turned out to be true. So recovery of mopping up of the weapons is another thing and then catching up all these pending cases and trying them and then getting them convicted in the court of law that is another one that JJ hospital matter we got him conviction for hanging that was converted into lifetime thing so that is there that kind of cases we took it up took it on fast trial follow it up and get them convicted So, then the next one is whenever they shot somebody or when they shot the police, encounter was not a policy, but if encounter happened, it happened as per law section 100 of the Indian Penal Code, but the whole Nadir as you described, the 101 people were shot and things like that, it happened because of the so-called encounter petition. One encounter went wrong, Javed Fowda in 1997. Abu Azmi of the Samajwadi party and a law person called Sebastian, they filed an encounter petition. The Bombay High Court asked the District Principal Saj called Justice Agiyar to inquire into that. He said not only that was a fake encounter and murder, 95 other incidents were also fake and murders. That's where the Mumbai police went into cold storage. All the so-called encounter specialists who were all heroes, they all went into hiding because they were to face the murder cases.

Top grade, all satellites, this one, that one, recording all that had happened that time. So it's a very well recorded, very well analyzed thing. In Mumbai, if you are coming back again, Mr. Hemant Karkare as ATS chief had called all the hotels on the Dharia Kinara and warned them in writing that this shop, that should shop, this close, close, close and all. Everything was obeyed. It's on record. He gave it in writing, they obeyed. But being hospitality industry, slowly, one by one, one by one, all those restrictions vanish. And when it actually happened, we were open like that. So if you are asking that intelligence was there or not, intelligence was there. Six pieces of intelligence had come. init_text: That's it. What were the steps that you put in place after you took over in order to keep the city safe?
resp_text: After that, again, imagination, you know, you can imagine 360 degrees attack could come immediately from the air, water, rail, road, anywhere. So you have to cover the city from 360 degrees. So we bought bulletproof boats, about 55 of them. and did patrolling there, whatever a policeman could do, coastal and all. The government of India spent humongous amount of money on improving navy and coast guard, power, purchase of boats and ships and commandos and various things like that. I brought commandos trainers from Israel after going to Israel. We brought the best of the weapons from all over the world and I bought seven simulators so that people can go on training, honing their skills in shooting. And they were one and a half crores each, seven such pieces I brought. Then I brought that bulletproof vehicles, 40 of them, that Mahindra jeeps which you see, marksman, 40 bulletproof vehicles. And 12 men sit there, they are all trained. We created five control rooms in the city where 100 trained commandos sit in five of them. So 500 of them ready in multiple places if attack takes place. Night also they are there. And we created a Force 1. Force 1 is a carbon copy of the NSG which came late for the Taj. NSG also is present here in Mumbai in Marol. So NSG is there, then equivalent of Force 1 is there and then our own commandos are there and our own QRT is there. Bulletproof vehicles are there, then for shooting and training those simulators are there. I conducted a 43,000 people's medical examination outside of government to check their medical health. I created the gymnasiums for becoming better health and things like that. And then we created a training center, Prerna Hall, where we can do training psychologically and otherwise and things like that. So multiple things were done at that time. and to create awareness amongst the people who are having low morale, I created four conferences where Mr. Abdul Kalam and KPS Gill, MK Narayanan and Rubero and others came. NCPA we had two programs and we had one in Dadar, one in Chembur. So, about 1200 common citizens came and attended and all, policemen also. We trained the policemen to be more, I wrote an SOP, Standard Operating Procedure. For example, all the officers, brave officers, about 26-11 I must put it on record, the bravery and the other things displayed, courage displayed by individual officers is exemplary. Like Sadanand Dattai went there to Kama Hospital, it's not his jurisdiction, he went there. Your Ashok Kamte went from Chembu to that place. It is also a jurisdiction. As per SOP they are not supposed to go but I wrote the SOP later. But then this shows that they were not afraid and they were not worrying about their life and the protection and things like that. They went ahead. One Ashok Pawar, a constable, he was going off duty from BT station in that Kasab and Iqbal were shooting 65 people. So one Havaldar RPF, Railway Protection Force, his gun got jammed. This man was in plain clothes, Ashok Pawar I'm mentioning. He could have gone home and lived. He went and told him, I'll set it right and he was doing it for him, that Kasab saw and shot him on the head and killed him on the spot. Isn't it exemplary? He was in plain clothes. He went and tried to set right things. Even that man who announced in the VT station, some Shinde I suppose, to save people and save lots of lives by announcing that terrorists are doing that. These are all exemplary people. Major Unnikrishnan and Gajendra Singh coming down from that A, where this Jewish rabbi and his wife were there. So all those things are exemplary courageous acts. So Mumbai police is not short of courageous people and things like that. They needed guidance, training, preparation and all that, you know, anticipation and also drills. We do plenty of drills. You asked me what we have done in the last 11-12 years, 13 years, plenty of drills have been done by force one and various other people.

resp_text: Young people madam, the entire society is willing to admire and promote and celebrate people who are endowed with hardworking nature. and honesty and risk-taking and decision-making capabilities. This all can be reduced to two words also. You need honest officers and we want officers who make decisions, not procrastinators and also not those corrupt people who are counting dollars all the time. And we must all know that all people are being watched and role models, they all become role models, either positive role model or negative role model. So we are all role models that way. Why is Mr. Rubiro being a celebrated copper? He is 94 years old and so many. Why am I repeatedly mentioning R. H. Mandonsa or Mr. Inamdar or Mr. V. K. Saraf or Mr. Bawe. This name may not be known to many people. But S. S. Jog, D. S. Soman, so many other officers of the S3 years. They are all men of sterling quality. Mr. S K Bapat, who was my joint director in the IB, who took me in the IB, he said, why did you join? He said so and I joined because of him. These are all people who are of sterling qualities and character. How do we remember them? How many years now they've gone, but still they are being remembered. Mr. Rivero commands so much respect even now.

So I took up science then, biology I didn't want to take because too much to read, too much to remember, just like it seems easier. I was more analytical than biological. resp_text: I think culinary schools and hospitality institutes are lacking in three aspects. especially around food. One is the cultural connotation and the cultural seats of cuisine are not explored. There is a logical cultural evolution to food that needs to be spoken about. for people to unlock many small questions and problems about food that they have. And most of them get solved saying, oh, OK, so samosa came from there. It became bigger because we put potatoes in it, because, you know, meat samosas are smaller. Now we're putting something that that has come to India. We're putting something vegetarian. We need to make it filling. It became bigger. So things get answered if you're able to understand the cultural evolution of food. I think that's lacking one. Macroeconomics, definitely. I think when I say macroeconomics, I mean the global economy of food is something that we never speak about. We don't speak enough about food spoilage globally, food wastage. We don't speak about agriculture, we don't speak about monocropping, we don't speak about agriculture and its impact on climate change, we don't speak about agricultural impact on water levels, overall agriculture and ecosystem imbalance that we are creating, particularly because of singular demand, you know. We don't speak about it at all. We start with the ingredient when it comes to our kitchen and we start talking about it. I think as chefs we need to understand the ingredient before it comes into our kitchen. 80% of our ecological problems are because of what's on our plate. It's basically that. We are creating an imbalance on the plate, which is causing an ecological imbalance, which needs to be spoken about at a broader agricultural macroeconomy versus demand conversation. So, yes, I think that conversation needs to happen in colleges, in catering and culinary schools. The third thing I feel that does not happen enough is celebration of our own food. I think, you know, very often because our kitchens are structured the French way, our education, culinary education is structured the Escoffier way. It's easy to break it down. It's easy to explain. Sometimes we take the shortcut of just using that and basing more or most of our examples in the West. We don't use examples from our kitchens as often to explain concepts, to explain kitchen organization, to explain the basics of kitchen. I think, yeah, I mean, a lot of it we are to blame because we don't have those books. We don't have, we didn't have an Escoffier who put it all together.

resp_text: When I was starting off in the restaurant business, I think that every restauranteur out there can relate to this. You felt very vulnerable. There's a complete maze and a labyrinth of licenses and no objection certificates that you need to navigate to be able to sell a sandwich. to get 36 different licenses. And for each license, you need four different NOCs. That takes up a considerable amount of your time, as you would possibly relate. And you are absolutely at the mercy of the bureaucratic environment that you operated in. any person could cancel your license. And if that meant that so many people would lose their jobs, everything that you worked for could go down the drain if you didn't participate in a system. For a while, I thought that, hey, this is how it works. And then after a while, I was like, yeah, this is how it works, but this is not how it should work. Because, I mean, the amount of employment that the hospitality industry is providing to the country, the amount of taxes that we're generating, Hospitality business is seven times the hotel business. Restaurants is 25 times the size of Bollywood. It's second only to the banking and the railways in employment generating capability. And I was like, where's the recognition? Forget the recognition, forget the awards. Why are we not being recognized as for what we truly are? As a credible community. Is what we are empowering people. You could take somebody and you could train them to be in the hospitality business in two days. Whereas every other business requires a lot of skilling. The restaurant business is a bridge between and the blue collar workers and the white collar workers, right? It is absolutely that bridge. And we felt that, you know, after some time I was like, listen, this needs to be stopped. Like we need to come together and we need to fight back. We need to push back. So, and I think that that resonated with a lot of people and everybody, you know, just felt that, look, you're not alone. We're here to fight back. We're here to speak up. And I think that, Culturally also, a restauranteur or even a restauranteur is viewed as a rich man's indulgence and not a cultural thing. Good people don't go to restaurants. You eat at home, you make thali, you keep bananas. What is the need to eat outside? You go out, you drink alcohol, you eat outside. You are a bad kind of people. So I think that needs to change. I think people mistake service for servility. And, you know, a server for a servant. And I saw us getting bashed all the time. Oh, they need to be taught a lesson in humility. How can they talk to a customer like that? But they themselves would go to a waiter and go... or not even look at a person in the eye. And I thought that all this needs to change. I think there needed to be a cultural change and that would not happen until we bound it together and kind of put a united front.

init_text: So very vocally, you've not been the biggest fan of delivery portals. And now with the massive pivot to delivery over in-house dining, especially post-COVID, what is your approach to food delivery?
resp_text: I think it's a misconception. I have never had anything against delivery business, per se. I think... They are non-competing businesses with each other. And I deeply appreciate the role aggregators have played in growing that segment of the business. What I am against is the tyranny of the aggregators, not the aggregators themselves. And I want there to be a level playing field. I want our agreements to be not unilateral. I want there to be fair play and fairness in the way it is conducted. And I think that we echo the same pain points of the entire industry. So we're not against delivery at all, because we don't think that dining out is competing with eating at home. They are two separate businesses. dining out will always remain dining out. And I think COVID really brought home this point because while all the pundits and all these tech pundits were predicting that, oh, you know, nobody's ever going to go and shop offline again and everything's going to happen online. Nobody's ever going to go to the restaurant again and everybody's going to, you know, order in. All that has just proven to be complete. It's been completely debunked. In fact, after COVID, People went back to restaurants like never before. People started travelling like never before. Malls were filled like never before. I think that you can never ever, in fact, what COVID has taught us is that you can never ever replace dining. And because dining out is not consuming food, right? Dining out is, it's not even an experience. It is a get together with your friends. It's a gossip session. It is a celebration of a little victory. It is celebrating a birthday. A anniversary is going somewhere to forget about your breakup. is going there to meet people. It is human behavior and that's never going to change. What delivery business is competing is that, okay, I've made food at home, it's very boring, so I'll eat outside. So delivery business is competing with your kitchen. It's not competing with the experience of dining out. So that's a misnomer. And I have nothing against delivery portals. They are all friends of mine. I think the NRAI is what stands in between complete annihilation of the industry and the tyranny of aggregators. And that needs to be kept in check. And I think that now Kabir and Sagar who have taken on the baton of NRAI are doing a great job with it as well. And it's just to protect the interests of the little guy. Like they're starting off, I think a 25% delivery charge, a 22% discount, and a 15% discovery charge, which is your marketing. So literally 60% is going to the aggregators. And aggregators with 60% of this entire ecosystem still are not making money. But a restauranteur is supposed to make money with only 40% margin. out of which 30%, as you would know, is food cost. So in 5%, you have to pay for your salaries, your rent. How is it going to work? How is it going to work? It's not. So we are here to talk sense to them.
